analysis.one_liner: Makes financial regulators prove trading limits won't burden bank competition before adopting them.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 32-22, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the Volcker Rule — the part of banking law that bans banks from trading for their own profit and from affiliating with hedge funds — to add new hurdles for regulators. Any agency writing or changing a rule under that section would have to weigh competition, efficiency, and capital formation, and could not adopt a rule that burdens competition unless it shows the burden is necessary. In practice, that gives big banks a new legal handle to slow down, weaken, or challenge limits on their proprietary trading.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks that engage in or near the line of proprietary trading gain, because regulators would face a mandatory competition and capital-formation analysis — and a prohibition on rules that burden competition — before adopting or changing trading restrictions. That raises the cost of regulation and gives regulated banks grounds to push back against stricter rules.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Federal Reserve, FDIC, SEC, and CFTC to consider whether any Volcker Rule regulation is necessary in the public interest and whether it promotes efficiency, competition, and capital formation before issuing or modifying it.

Bars the agencies from adopting a rule that imposes a burden on competition unless the burden is necessary or appropriate, and requires them to publicly explain any such burden in the rule's statement of basis and purpose.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on the Volcker Rule's protections bear the risk: the rule is meant to stop banks from gambling for their own accounts with federally insured deposits, and a weaker or slower rulemaking process leaves taxpayers more exposed if a bank's trading losses threaten it.

drawbacks.text: The bill does more than require consideration: it prohibits agencies from adopting any rule that burdens competition unless the burden is necessary or appropriate, which could be used to challenge or delay rules that curb risky proprietary trading at banks backed by federal deposit insurance.
Supporters argue the added analysis is a fair check that regulators weigh the costs of trading restrictions to markets and capital formation, not a way to gut the rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Whatever its merits as a rulemaking-procedure bill, its practical effect would fall almost entirely on one side of the ledger: it targets a single consumer- and taxpayer-protection rule and hands regulated banks a new procedural weapon against it, while offering ordinary people no offsetting benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill at a July 2014 markup by a 32-22 vote, but no further action was ever taken and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 16, 2014 and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit held a hearing on July 15, 2014.
On July 30, 2014, the committee considered the bill in markup and ordered it reported by a vote of 32 to 22.
No further action followed; the bill never reached the House floor and expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The financial regulators the bill targeted keep their existing discretion to write and tighten Volcker Rule trading restrictions without the added competition bar, and the taxpayer protections the bill aimed to make harder to enforce remain in place unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Sean Duffy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the Financial Services Committee.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee Republicans
for.what_they_did: Provided the 32 votes to order the bill reported out of committee at the July 30, 2014 markup.

against.name: 22 House Financial Services Committee members
against.what_they_did: Voted against ordering the bill reported at the July 30, 2014 markup.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sole cosponsor was a Republican and the committee approved it 32-22 under a Republican majority, but the sources do not give a party breakdown of the markup vote.

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill adds a mandatory competition and capital-formation test — and a bar on competition-burdensome rules — to every regulation issued under the Volcker Rule's proprietary-trading ban, giving banks a new way to slow, weaken, or challenge limits on trading with insured deposits.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity funds
industries.note: The Volcker Rule restricts banks' relationships with these funds; easier-to-challenge rulemaking could loosen those restrictions over time, though the bill does not change the underlying prohibition directly.

industries.industry: Federal financial regulators (Fed, FDIC, SEC, CFTC)
industries.note: The agencies would lose discretion: they could not adopt a rule that burdens competition without documenting its necessity, adding a legal vulnerability to every trading-rule they write or modify.
